title: Confident Leaders Who Drastically Change Their Style When Communicating Upward
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Notes essay examines leaders who are forceful with their own teams but become obsequious in front of high-status people. Some style adjustment is normal and reads as respect, but the trouble starts when the shift becomes a transformation: the confident voice goes quiet, positions soften into questions, and agreement and praise come early and often. The piece argues that leaders who orient to power rather than to values often kiss up and kick down. The cost grows over time, because senior leaders come to discount automatic agreement and lose the independent, candid view they most need, and team members learn that their leader's views are negotiable and their concerns will not survive the trip upstairs. The prescription is to adapt delivery to the room while keeping substance and treatment of people constant, since that consistency is the foundation of leadership credibility.
points: Leaders can be confident downward and deferential upward, and the confidence they show their teams often does not travel up.
Leaders who orient to power instead of values tend to kiss up and kick down, treating people according to what they can do for them.
Automatic agreement with senior leaders gets discounted and eventually recasts earlier praise as calculated and empty.
Adjust delivery to the room but never the substance: beliefs about issues and how people should be treated should not change with the title across the table.
quotes: Some style adjustment is normal. People display status in how they express themselves and engage with others.
What makes this striking is that many of these leaders are confident, even forceful, with their own teams. The confidence is real. It just doesn’t travel upward.

Positions they defended an hour earlier soften into questions. They agree early and often, and praise ideas they would have challenged if a peer had offered them. They are not adapting to the room. They are surrendering to it.
When power is the reference point, how a leader treats someone depends on what that person can do for them.

In the short run, senior leaders enjoy the agreement and welcome the praise. But the leader who consistently defers to status gives up the very thing senior leaders need most from them, which is an independent and candid view.

Once high-status leaders notice that the agreement is automatic, it stops carrying weight. The junior leader’s input gets discounted, and their judgment gets questioned, especially when they are not in the room.
The answer for leaders is not to stop adapting to people. Good leaders read every room and adjust their delivery to fit the situation. What they don’t adjust is their substance.
That consistency is not stubbornness or inflexibility. It is the foundation of leadership credibility.
